docs.title: alma-affect-kit v1.0.0
docs.text:
alma-affect-kit is a faithful Python implementation of ALMA, A Layered Model of Affect (Patrick Gebhard, DFKI; AAMAS 2005), packaged as a reusable simulation engine and toolkit for affect modelling. It models three interacting layers of affect, emotions, moods and personality, driven by world events.

You create an engine and populate it with characters. Each character has a Big Five personality profile and may also include a set of appraisal rules that define how it interprets events from its own perspective. During a session, you provide the engine with occurrences such as events, actions, displays, or direct appraisals, and advance the simulation over time.

Each appraisal can trigger emotions that fade as time passes. While they remain active, these emotions shape the character's mood within PAD space. Once the situation settles, the mood gradually returns toward its baseline state. A character's dominant emotion and mood can then be expressed in everyday terms, such as "slightly hostile" or "moderately exuberant," making it possible to condition behaviour on those affective states.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• P. Gebhard. ALMA, A Layered Model of Affect. AAMAS 2005.
  • P. Gebhard, M. Kipp, M. Klesen, T. Rist. Adding the Emotional Dimension to Scripting Character Dialogues. IVA 2003.
  • P. Gebhard, M. Klesen, T. Rist. Coloring Multi-Character Conversations through the Expression of Emotions. ADS 2004.
  • A. Ortony, G. L. Clore, A. Collins. The Cognitive Structure of Emotions. Cambridge University Press, 1988.
  • A. Mehrabian. Pleasure-arousal-dominance: A general framework for describing and measuring individual differences in temperament. Current Psychology 14, 1996.
  • A. Mehrabian. Analysis of the Big-five Personality Factors in Terms of the PAD Temperament Model. Australian Journal of Psychology 48(2), 1996.

Important: alma-affect-kit is an independent reimplementation based on the published papers and is not affiliated with DFKI. ALMA is the original work of Patrick Gebhard (DFKI). While this implementation aims to faithfully reproduce the published model, it may contain deviations and cannot guarantee scientific accuracy. See Fidelity Notes for further details.

AI Disclaimer

In this project, AI was used to extract information, generate code, and documentation under human guidance and oversight. It was used in various personal projects and subsequently shared with the open-source community. All documents and most code were human-reviewed and updated after the initial AI generation, but there may still be overlooked or sloppy parts.

docs.text: Everything below is importable from the top-level package alma_affect_kit

docs.text:
One character's layered affective state (created via add_character).

docs.title: AffectConfig
docs.text: All model parameters with publication defaults; see Configuration for the full table. validate() re-checks after field assignment. MoodReturnMode.IDLE / .ALWAYS name the two return modes.

docs.title: Personality
docs.text: Symbol Description Personality(openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism) Frozen Big Five profile, traits clamped to [-1, 1]; as_dict() TRAITS The five trait names default_mood(personality, weights=None) -> PAD Mehrabian's Big Five → PAD regression (clamped into the cube) emotion_baseline(personality, emotion, table=None) -> float Baseline intensity of one emotion type DEFAULT_PERSONALITY_TO_MOOD The regression weights DEFAULT_PERSONALITY_BASELINES The default baseline weight table

docs.title: Mood dynamics (lower level)
docs.text:
Symbol Description VirtualEmotionCenter(position: PAD, intensity) The VEC compute_emotion_center(emotions, config) -> VirtualEmotionCenter \| None VEC of the active emotions update_mood(mood, default_mood, vec, dt, config) -> PAD One pull/push or return step (result clamped into the cube)

These are what CharacterAffect.update() uses internally; they are exposed for custom integrations and testing.

docs.title: Appraisal
docs.text: Appraisal is how world input becomes emotion. The outcome of one appraisal is an emotion eliciting condition (EEC), a bundle of variables describing the situation. The signs of the variables select which of the 24 emotion types are elicited; the absolute values determine the intensities.

docs.title: EEC variables
docs.text:
Variable Range Meaning desirability [-1, 1] How (un)desirable an event is for the appraising character desirability_for_other [-1, 1] How (un)desirable an event is for another character praiseworthiness [-1, 1] How praise- or blameworthy an action is agency None / "self" / "other" Who performed the action (None counts as "other") appealingness [-1, 1] How (un)appealing an object is liking [-1, 1] How attracted the character is to the other person/object likelihood [0, 1] Degree of belief that an anticipated event will occur realization [0, 1] Degree of belief that an anticipated event has occurred prospect None / "confirmed" / "disconfirmed" Outcome status of an anticipated event cause str Free-text elicitor, carried onto the emotions

Out-of-range values raise ValueError at construction.

docs.title: Elicitation reference
docs.text:
Where two variables participate, the intensity is the mean of their absolute values.

Events (well-being / prospect-based):

Condition Emotion Intensity desirability > 0 Joy |d| desirability < 0 Distress |d| d > 0, likelihood set Hope mean(|d|, l) d < 0, likelihood set Fear mean(|d|, l) d > 0, prospect confirmed Satisfaction mean(|d|, r) d < 0, prospect confirmed FearsConfirmed mean(|d|, r) d > 0, prospect disconfirmed Disappointment mean(|d|, r) d < 0, prospect disconfirmed Relief mean(|d|, r)

Events happening to others (fortunes-of-others):

Condition Emotion desirability_for_other > 0, liking ≥ 0 HappyFor desirability_for_other > 0, liking < 0 Resentment desirability_for_other < 0, liking ≥ 0 Pity desirability_for_other < 0, liking < 0 Gloating

Actions (attribution):

Condition Emotion praiseworthiness > 0, agency self Pride praiseworthiness < 0, agency self Shame praiseworthiness > 0, agency other Admiration praiseworthiness < 0, agency other Reproach

Compounds (well-being × attribution, no prospect)

  • Both desirability and praiseworthiness set in one EEC
Condition Emotion d > 0, p > 0, agency self Gratification d > 0, p > 0, agency other Gratitude d < 0, p < 0, agency self Remorse d < 0, p < 0, agency other Anger

Objects (attraction):

Condition Emotion appealingness > 0 Liking appealingness < 0 Disliking appealingness > 0 and liking > 0 Love appealingness < 0 and liking < 0 Hate

docs.title: Basic appraisal tags
docs.text:
The papers define symbolic abbreviations for common EECs (IVA'03, Table 1), available as helper constructors with the papers' default degrees ("moderately" = 0.5; likely = 0.75, unlikely = 0.25):

Tag / constructor EEC it builds good_event(0.5) / bad_event(-0.5) desirability ±0.5 good_likely_future_event(0.5, 0.75) / bad_likely_future_event desirability ±0.5, likelihood 0.75 good_unlikely_future_event(0.5, 0.25) / bad_unlikely_future_event desirability ±0.5, likelihood 0.25 good_act_self(0.5) / bad_act_self(-0.5) praiseworthiness ±0.5, agency self good_act_other(0.5) / bad_act_other(-0.5) praiseworthiness ±0.5, agency other nice_thing(0.5) / nasty_thing(-0.5) appealingness ±0.5 prospect_confirmed(d) / prospect_disconfirmed(d) the anticipated event's outcome event_for_other(d, liking=0.5) fortunes-of-others

Signs are normalised. E.g. good_event(0.7) and good_event(-0.7) both mean desirability +0.7.

docs.title: Merging: how compounds arise
docs.text:
An appraisal rule may emit several basic appraisals for one input, the paper's example: an "attack" is a bad event and a blameworthy act of another (Fig. 4). OCC treats these as one situation appraised along several dimensions, which is what elicits the compound emotions. An attack appraised as a bad event (desirability −0.5) plus a blameworthy act of another (praiseworthiness −0.3) therefore elicits three emotions at once: Distress 0.5, Reproach 0.3 and the compound Anger 0.4 (before personality bias).

Merging is deliberately conservative, two EECs merge only when they describe the same situation:

  • no variable set on both sides with different values,
  • no explicit agency disagreement,
  • equal causes (or one/both absent),
  • the same event structure, an actual event never merges with a prospective or confirmed one (that would turn Joy into Hope).

Incompatible EECs stay separate and elicit independently. Pass merge=False to appraise() to disable merging entirely.

docs.title: Personality bias
docs.text: Each elicited intensity is raised by the character's personality baseline for that emotion type and clamped to [0, 1]; the emotion then decays back to the baseline. Disable with AffectConfig(apply_personality_bias=False).

docs.title: The rule system
docs.text:
A character's profile bundles its personality with subjective appraisal rules, the Python counterpart of AffectML's rule classes:

Rule class Matches Scopes on_event(name, *eecs) named events/objects (perceive_event) on_act(act, scope, *eecs, performer=None) (dialog) acts (perceive_act) self, direct, indirect on_emotion_display(display, scope, *eecs, performer=None) visible emotion cues (perceive_emotion_display) self, other on_mood_display(display, scope, *eecs, performer=None) visible mood cues (perceive_mood_display) self, other

Dispatch for an act:

  • the performer matches its self rules,
  • the target its direct rules,
  • and everyone else their indirect (listener) rules.

A rule with performer="Sven" only fires for Sven's acts. All appraisals from one matched input share the input as their cause and are merged as described above.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Every parameter of the model is configurable through AffectConfig. The defaults are the publication values, an unconfigured engine behaves exactly as described in the AAMAS'05 paper. You can construct a configuration in code, or load one from a YAML (or JSON) file; characters' personality and rules profiles are both configurable.

docs.title: Emotion parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Constraint What it controls emotion_decay_time 20 s > 0 How long an elicited emotion takes to fade back to its baseline. Shorter values make characters flare and settle quickly; longer values let single events cast a longer emotional shadow, and, because active emotions drive the mood, also deepen each event's effect on mood. decay_function linear linear, exponential, tanhyp The shape of the fade. Linear falls steadily. Exponential drops fast and trails off, a sharp reaction that quickly loses force. Tangens hyperbolicus is an S-curve: the emotion holds near full strength briefly, falls through the middle, then eases out, the most natural-looking for visible expressions. dominant_emotion_threshold 0.4 0 – 1 Emotions should not visibly drive behaviour a priori: only the strongest active emotion above this threshold is reported as the dominant emotion. Lower it and characters emote at every little thing; raise it and only strong feelings show. apply_personality_bias on on/off Whether personality baselines raise elicited intensities (an extravert feels joy more strongly). Turn off for personality-neutral emotion strength.

docs.title: Mood parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Constraint What it controls mood_change_time 600 s (10 min) > 0 The mood's responsiveness to emotions: the time a full-intensity emotion centre needs to move the mood between two adjacent octant centres. Smaller values give volatile, fast-swinging moods; the default gives the paper's deliberately inert medium-term mood. mood_change_distance 1.0 > 0 The PAD distance the mood covers in mood_change_time. The paper calibrates on "one mood octant centre to another" without naming the pair; adjacent centres are 1.0 apart (default), centres across a face √2, opposite centres √3. Only the speed changes; the dynamics are otherwise identical. mood_return_time 1200 s (20 min) > 0 How quickly a disturbed mood drifts home: the time to travel the longest octant distance (√3) back to the default mood. Governs how long a bad stretch lingers after the events stop. mood_return_mode idle idle, always Idle: the homeward drift acts only while no emotions are active (the paper's reading, while emotions live, they own the mood). Always: the drift is superimposed on the emotional pull, giving a slightly stickier, more anchored mood. vec_intensity_weighted off on/off How the emotion centre's position is computed from the active emotions: the plain average of their PAD points (the paper's reading), or an average weighted by intensity so stronger emotions pull the centre towards themselves.

docs.title: Timing and mapping tables
docs.text:
Parameter Default What it controls update_period 0.5 s The step size used by step() and run(), the paper's 500 ms affect rate. Must be positive. emotion_pad_map Table 2 of the paper Where each of the 24 emotion types sits in PAD space, i.e. which mood each emotion pulls towards. Entries you provide merge over the defaults. personality_to_mood Mehrabian's regression The Big Five → default-mood weights, per PAD axis. Must map exactly the three axes; trait names are validated. personality_baselines see Fidelity Notes The Big Five → per-emotion baseline weights: which traits make which emotions run hot at rest.

Validation happens on construction and again if a file is loaded; violations raise a specific errors.

docs.title: Value ranges throughout the engine
docs.text: Quantity Range Handling Big Five traits −1 to +1 clamped Appraisal variables (desirability, praiseworthiness, appealingness, liking, desirability-for-other) −1 to +1 error outside Likelihood, realization 0 to 1 error outside Emotion intensities 0 to 1 clamped; never below the personality baseline Mood (each PAD axis) −1 to +1 kept inside the cube by the engine

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.text:
Configuration and character files are YAML documents whose structure mirrors the library's own field names, with times in seconds. A configuration file sets any subset of the parameters above; a character file holds a name, a personality and the appraisal rule book (basic event rules, act rules with their scope and optional performer, and emotion/mood display rules). JSON is accepted with the identical structure (.json files are parsed strictly as JSON; JSON is otherwise a subset of YAML), and Python dicts can be passed directly. A mistyped path raises a file-not-found error rather than being mistaken for document content.

Complete, commented file templates, and the code that loads them, are on the Examples page; ready-to-copy files ship in the repository's examples/ directory.

docs.title: From AffectML to YAML
docs.text:
The paper specifies its configuration in AffectML, an XML-based language (its Figures 3 and 4). This library does not read XML; instead every AffectML construct has a YAML equivalent, so the paper's documents translate one-to-one. The only systematic change is the time unit: AffectML uses milliseconds, YAML uses seconds.

AffectComputation document → configuration file

AffectML YAML <EmotionDecay time="20000"> emotion_decay_time: 20.0 <EmotionDecay period="500"> (also <MoodReturn period>) update_period: 0.5 <EmotionDecay function="linear"> decay_function: linear <EmotionBaseline threshold="0.4"> dominant_emotion_threshold: 0.4 <MoodReturn time="1200000"> mood_return_time: 1200.0 the mood change time (stated only in the paper's text) mood_change_time: 600.0 <MoodRelations><EmotionRelation name="Anger" p a d/> emotion_pad_map: {Anger: [p, a, d]} <PersonalityRelations><PleasureRelation extra agree neur/> personality_to_mood: {pleasure: {extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism}} <ArousalRelation> / <DominanceRelation> personality_to_mood: {arousal: {...}, dominance: {...}} <RealtimeOutput> / <FileLog> not applicable, output is read programmatically via affect_output()

CharacterAffect document → character file

AffectML YAML <CharacterAffect name="Valerie"> name: Valerie <Personality open con extra agree neur/> personality: {openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism} <Basic><GoodEvent desirability="0.7"/></Basic> (input = the tag name) basic: {GoodEvent: [{tag: GoodEvent, desirability: 0.7}]} a basic rule for a named event basic: {SunIsShining: [{tag: GoodEvent, desirability: 0.7}]} <SelfAct type="Calm"> acts: [{act: Calm, scope: self, appraisals: [...]}] <DirectAct type="Attack" performer="Sven"> acts: [{act: Attack, scope: direct, performer: Sven, appraisals: [...]}] <IndirectAct type="..."> acts: [{act: ..., scope: indirect, ...}] <SelfEmotion emotion="ReproachDisplay"> / <OtherEmotion> emotion_displays: [{display: ReproachDisplay, scope: self \| other, performer?, appraisals}] <SelfMood mood="..."> / <OtherMood> mood_displays: [{display: ..., scope: self \| other, ...}] rule body <GoodActSelf agency="self" praiseworthiness="0.5"/> {tag: GoodActSelf, agency: self, praiseworthiness: 0.5} (the redundant agency may be kept or dropped) any basic appraisal tag element {tag: <TagName>, <its degree>} monitored, docu attributes not applicable (tooling metadata)

The paper's own Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 documents, translated this way, are part of the test suite and reproduce the paper's attack scenario (Distress, Reproach and Anger for Valerie).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: All the runnable code in one place. The concepts behind each snippet are explained in Usage, Appraisal, Simulation and Configuration.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from alma_affect_kit import AffectEngine, Personality, good_event

engine = AffectEngine()                       # publication defaults

valerie = engine.add_character("Valerie", Personality(
    openness=0.4, conscientiousness=0.8, extraversion=0.6,
    agreeableness=0.3, neuroticism=0.4))

print(valerie.default_mood)                   # PAD(P=+0.38, A=-0.08, D=+0.50)
print(valerie.mood_word)                      # 'moderate relaxed'

engine.appraise("Valerie", good_event(0.7, cause="sun is shining"))
engine.update(0.5)                            # advance 500 ms
print(valerie.dominant_emotion)               # ActiveEmotion(Joy, ...)

engine.run(25.0)                              # emotions decay (20 s default)
print(valerie.active_emotions)                # []

docs.title: Direct appraisals
docs.text:
from alma_affect_kit import (good_event, bad_event, bad_act_other,
                         bad_likely_future_event, prospect_disconfirmed,
                         event_for_other, nice_thing, EEC)

engine.appraise("Valerie", good_event(0.7))                  # Joy
engine.appraise("Valerie", bad_likely_future_event(-0.8))    # Fear
engine.appraise("Valerie", prospect_disconfirmed(-0.8))      # Relief
engine.appraise("Valerie", event_for_other(-0.6, liking=0.7))  # Pity
engine.appraise("Valerie", nice_thing(0.6, liking=0.8))      # Liking + Love

# one situation appraised along two dimensions -> the compound Anger
engine.appraise("Valerie", [bad_event(-0.5), bad_act_other(-0.3)])
# -> Distress 0.5, Reproach 0.3, Anger 0.4   (before personality bias)

# raw EECs give full control
engine.appraise("Valerie", EEC(desirability=0.6,
                               praiseworthiness=0.4))        # + Gratitude

docs.title: Building a rule book
docs.text:
from alma_affect_kit import (AppraisalRules, good_event, bad_event,
                         bad_act_other, event_for_other)

valerie_rules = (AppraisalRules()
    .on_event("SunIsShining", good_event(0.7))
    .on_act("Attack", "direct", bad_event(-0.5), bad_act_other(-0.3),
            performer="Sven")               # only when Sven attacks her
    .on_act("GoodJoke", "indirect", good_event(0.3))   # as a listener
    .on_emotion_display("BlushOfShame", "other", event_for_other(-0.3)))

engine.add_character("Valerie", personality, valerie_rules)

docs.title: Perceiving world input
docs.text:
engine.perceive_event("SunIsShining")       # everyone appraises it
engine.perceive_act("Attack", performer="Sven", addressee="Valerie")
engine.perceive_emotion_display("BlushOfShame", performer="Sven")
engine.perceive_mood_display("NervousIdle", performer="Sven")

# scope an input to the characters who can perceive it
engine.perceive_act("Whisper", performer="Sven", addressee="Valerie",
                    characters=["Sven", "Valerie"])

Every call returns what it elicited, per character: {"Valerie": [ActiveEmotion(Distress, ...), ...]}.

docs.title: Reading affect for behaviour
docs.text:
from alma_affect_kit import MoodOctant

octant = character.mood.octant
if octant is MoodOctant.HOSTILE:
    reply = pick_short_harsh_line()
elif octant is MoodOctant.RELAXED:
    reply = pick_lengthy_friendly_line()

if (dominant := character.dominant_emotion):
    face.show(dominant.type.label, dominant.intensity)

snapshot = character.affect_output()     # JSON-able, for saves/telemetry

docs.title: Game-loop integration
docs.text:
# fixed-timestep affect alongside a variable frame rate
AFFECT_STEP = 0.5                        # the paper's 500 ms period
accumulator = 0.0

def game_tick(frame_dt):
    global accumulator
    world.simulate(frame_dt)
    accumulator += frame_dt
    while accumulator >= AFFECT_STEP:
        engine.update(AFFECT_STEP)
        accumulator -= AFFECT_STEP
    render(world, engine.affect_output())

def on_player_insulted_npc(npc, player):
    engine.perceive_act("Insult", performer=player.name,
                        addressee=npc.name)

Calling engine.update(frame_dt) directly every frame works just as well, per-frame updates are cheap.

docs.title: Configuring the engine in code
docs.text:
from alma_affect_kit import AffectConfig, AffectEngine, DecayFunction

config = AffectConfig(emotion_decay_time=60.0,
                      decay_function=DecayFunction.EXPONENTIAL,
                      mood_change_time=120.0,
                      mood_return_mode="always")
engine = AffectEngine(config)

docs.title: Loading configuration and character files
docs.text:
from alma_affect_kit import AffectEngine, load_config, load_character

engine = AffectEngine(load_config("affect.yaml"))
engine.add_character(*load_character("valerie.yaml"))
engine.add_character(*load_character("sven.json"))    # JSON works too

docs.title: YAML configuration template (times in seconds)
docs.text:
# affect.yaml: all values shown are the defaults
emotion_decay_time: 20.0
decay_function: linear            # linear | exponential | tanhyp
dominant_emotion_threshold: 0.4
update_period: 0.5
mood_change_time: 600.0
mood_return_time: 1200.0
mood_return_mode: idle            # idle | always
vec_intensity_weighted: false
emotion_pad_map:                  # optional overrides, merged over Table 2
  Anger: [-0.51, 0.59, 0.25]
personality_to_mood:              # optional per-axis overrides
  pleasure: {extraversion: 0.21, agreeableness: 0.59, neuroticism: 0.19}
personality_baselines:            # optional per-emotion overrides
  Joy: {extraversion: 0.15, agreeableness: 0.10}

docs.title: YAML character template
docs.text:
name: Valerie
personality: {openness: 0.4, conscientiousness: 0.8, extraversion: 0.6,
              agreeableness: 0.3, neuroticism: 0.4}
appraisal:
  basic:
    SunIsShining:
      - {tag: GoodEvent, desirability: 0.7}
  acts:
    - act: Disturb
      scope: direct               # self | direct | indirect
      performer: Sven             # optional filter
      appraisals:
        - {tag: BadEvent, desirability: -0.5}
        - {tag: BadActOther, praiseworthiness: -0.6}
  emotion_displays:
    - display: ReproachDisplay
      scope: self                 # self | other
      appraisals:
        - {tag: BadEvent, desirability: -0.3}
  mood_displays: []

An appraisal entry is either {tag: <BasicTagName>, ...} or a raw EEC such as {desirability: -0.5, praiseworthiness: -0.3, agency: other}.

docs.title: The paper's Fig. 4 character in YAML
docs.text:
The AAMAS'05 paper's own example character specification (an AffectML document), translated one-to-one, see the mapping table on the Configuration page:

name: Valerie
personality: {openness: 0.4, conscientiousness: 0.8, extraversion: 0.6,
              agreeableness: 0.3, neuroticism: 0.4}
appraisal:
  basic:
    GoodEvent:                              # paper form: input = tag name
      - {tag: GoodEvent, desirability: 0.7}
  acts:
    - act: Calm                             # <SelfAct type="Calm">
      scope: self
      appraisals:
        - {tag: GoodActSelf, praiseworthiness: 0.5}
    - act: Attack                           # <DirectAct type="Attack"
      scope: direct                         #            performer="Sven">
      performer: Sven
      appraisals:
        - {tag: BadEvent, desirability: -0.5}
        - {tag: BadActOther, praiseworthiness: -0.3}
  emotion_displays:
    - display: ReproachDisplay              # <SelfEmotion emotion=...>
      scope: self
      appraisals:
        - {tag: BadEvent, desirability: -0.3}

docs.title: Shipped example scripts
docs.text:
The repository's examples/ directory contains ready-to-run material:

File What it shows examples/quickstart.py One character: appraisals, decay, a mood arc, the return to the default mood examples/virtualhuman.py The paper's Valerie-and-Sven lesson scenario, loading profiles from files examples/affect.yaml Commented configuration template with every parameter at its publication default examples/valerie.yaml Valerie's profile: personality, event, act and display rules examples/sven.yaml Sven's profile

docs.title: Fidelity Notes
docs.text:
This library reproduces every quantitative parameter published in the AAMAS'05 paper and its EmotionEngine companion papers (IVA'03, ADS'04). This page records exactly what is taken from the papers verbatim, and the documented choices made where the papers are silent or inconsistent. Everything in the second category is configurable.

How this was verified. All 24 rows of Table 2 (PAD values and octants), all 8 octant names of Table 1, all nine Big Five → PAD regression coefficients, the paper's worked personality example and the Fig. 3 defaults were cross-checked programmatically against the text extracted from the published PDF, and are pinned in the test suite in full (not sampled). Readers are encouraged to repeat the comparison against the paper themselves; the constants live in emotion.py, personality.py and config.py.

docs.title: Taken verbatim from the publications
docs.text: Element Source The 24 emotion types and their PAD mapping AAMAS'05, Table 2 The eight mood octant names AAMAS'05, Table 1 Mood strength = norm of the PAD vector, √3 in three equal parts (slightly / moderate / fully) AAMAS'05, §3 Big Five → PAD default-mood regression (all coefficients) AAMAS'05, §3 (Mehrabian 1996) The worked personality example: (0.4, 0.8, 0.6, 0.3, 0.4) → (0.38, −0.08, 0.50), Relaxed AAMAS'05, §3, a test anchor Emotion decay 20 s, linear, 500 ms period; threshold 0.4 AAMAS'05, Fig. 3 (see the note on the threshold's meaning below) Three decay functions are named: linear, exponential, tangens hyperbolicus IVA'03 / ADS'04 (their exact curves are not published, see below) Mood change time 10 min (octant centre to octant centre) AAMAS'05, §3 Mood return time 20 min (over √3) AAMAS'05, §3 Virtual emotion centre = centre of active emotions, intensity = average intensity, max 1.0 AAMAS'05, §3 Pull phase / push phase semantics AAMAS'05, §3 + Fig. 2 EEC variables: desirability, praiseworthiness, appealingness, liking, likelihood, realization; signs select the emotion, magnitudes the intensity ADS'04, §3.2 Basic appraisal tags (good/bad event, likely/unlikely future, act self/other, nice/nasty thing) IVA'03, Table 1 Rule hierarchy: basic, act (self/direct/indirect), emotion display, mood display AAMAS'05, §4 The extravert joy baseline = 0.15 anchor IVA'03 / ADS'04 AffectML document semantics (AffectComputation, CharacterAffect), expressed in YAML AAMAS'05, Figs. 3–4

docs.title: Emotion intensity combination
docs.text: The papers say the absolute values of the EEC variables determine the intensities but give no formula for emotions with two contributing variables (hope, fear, the confirmations, fortunes-of-others, the compounds, love/hate). Choice: the mean of the absolute values of the participating variables.

docs.title: Personality baseline table
docs.text: Only the joy = 0.15 anchor is published, plus qualitative guidance (positive emotions rise with extraversion and agreeableness, negative with neuroticism; conscientiousness and openness influence the attribution and attraction groups). Choice: positive emotions get weights {extraversion: 0.15, agreeableness: 0.10}, negative {neuroticism: 0.15}, with {conscientiousness: 0.05} added for attribution/compound emotions and {openness: 0.05} for attraction emotions; baselines clamp at 0. Override any of it via AffectConfig.personality_baselines.

docs.title: Decay curve shapes
docs.text: Only the names of the three decay functions are published. Choice: linear falls to zero at the decay time; exponential is exp(−5·t/T) (≈0.7 % remaining at the decay time, then cut to zero); tangens hyperbolicus is a normalised 1 − tanh(6·t/T − 3) S-curve. All three reach 1 at t = 0 and 0 at t = T; the intermediate shape is ours.

docs.title: Decay towards the baseline
docs.text: IVA'03 says personality biases emotions with a baseline intensity (extravert joy baseline 0.15, introvert 0.0). Choice: the baseline is treated as the emotion's resting level, elicited intensities are raised by it and decay back to it, not to zero. With apply_personality_bias=False every baseline is zero and emotions decay to zero.

docs.title: The meaning of the 0.4 threshold
docs.text: Fig. 3 names the element EmotionBaseline threshold="0.4", while the companion papers describe a threshold that "the most dominant emotion" must exceed "to have an impact on the character's behaviour". Choice: the value is read as that behaviour threshold (dominant_emotion_threshold); it does not gate whether an emotion influences the mood.

docs.title: Emotion decay time: 20 s vs "for example, 1 minute"
docs.text: The Fig. 3 document sets EmotionDecay time="20000"; the running text mentions decay "over a certain amount of time (for example, 1 minute)". Choice: the document value (20 s) is the default.

docs.title: Which octant centres define the mood change time
docs.text: The paper calibrates the pull/push speed on the time "to move a current mood from one mood octant centre to another one" without naming the pair. Choice: adjacent centres (distance 1.0) by default; the distance is exposed as mood_change_distance (√2 across a face, √3 for opposite centres). Only the speed scale changes.

docs.title: Unspecified liking in fortunes-of-others appraisals
docs.text: When an event concerning another character is appraised without a liking value, OCC needs a sign to choose between happy-for/pity and resentment/gloating. Choice: unspecified liking counts as mildly positive (0.5).

docs.title: Mood return time: 10 vs 20 minutes
docs.text: The paper's running text says the mood return time "currently is 20 minutes" while its Fig. 3 example document shows MoodReturn time="600000" (10 minutes). Choice: the text value (1200 s) is the default.

docs.title: Mood strength boundary
docs.text: The paper labels its default-mood example (norm ≈ 0.633) slightly relaxed, although by its own thirds-of-√3 rule (boundary ≈ 0.577) it is just inside moderate, presumably rounding. Choice: the stated rule is followed exactly, so that example reads moderate relaxed here.

docs.title: Pull/push geometry
docs.text: The paper describes pull/push in prose and a 2-D figure. Choice: "between the zero point and the VEC" is implemented as the mood's projection onto the origin→VEC ray not yet reaching the VEC's distance; pull moves straight towards the VEC, push moves radially outward (deeper into the mood's current octant), clamped to the cube. Speed is the published calibration: vec_intensity / mood_change_time PAD units per second.

docs.title: Mood return while emotions are active
docs.text: The paper states the return tendency but not whether it applies during active emotions. Choice: default mood_return_mode="idle" (return only when no VEC exists, otherwise the two forces of comparable magnitude would largely cancel); "always" is available.

docs.title: Virtual emotion centre averaging
docs.text: "The virtual emotion centre of all currently active emotions" is read as the plain average of their PAD points (the paper assigns intensity a separate role: the average of intensities). Choice: plain average by default; vec_intensity_weighted=True switches to an intensity-weighted position.

docs.title: EEC merging for compound emotions
docs.text: OCC's compound emotions (anger, remorse, gratitude, gratification) require desirability and praiseworthiness appraised for one situation. The paper's Fig. 4 shows an attack appraised as BadEvent + BadActOther within one rule but doesn't state the combination mechanics. Choice: basic appraisals emitted for the same input are merged into one EEC when compatible, same cause, same event structure (actual vs prospective vs confirmed), no variable set on both sides with different values, no explicit agency disagreement. merge=False disables it.

docs.title: Sub-baseline elicitations
docs.text: Unspecified in the papers. Choice: an elicitation weaker than the personality baseline is raised to the baseline and stays active for the decay time (rather than being dropped), so mild stimuli still reach the mood dynamics.

docs.title: AffectML represented in YAML
docs.text: The paper defines AffectML as an XML language. This library keeps AffectML's semantics, the global computation parameters, the personality definition and the complete appraisal rule hierarchy, but represents documents in YAML (JSON accepted), with times in seconds rather than milliseconds. Every AffectML construct has a one-to-one YAML equivalent (mapping table on the Configuration page); the paper's own Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 documents are part of the test suite in translated form. Two things go slightly beyond the paper's schema: the mood change time is a first-class parameter (the paper states it only in prose), and basic rules can be keyed by an arbitrary event name in addition to the paper's tag-name form.

docs.title: Beyond the paper's scope (engineering)
docs.text:
• Strict validation everywhere (value ranges, unknown keys/tags/fields, trait-name typos), load-time ValueError rather than silent drift.
  • Exact PAD vector algebra; the mood is clamped into the cube only at assignment points.
  • Deterministic dt-driven stepping instead of a wall-clock thread.
  • The paper's future-work items are not implemented (and noted here for honesty): mood does not yet influence emotion intensity, appraisal rules are static at runtime, and there is no group-mood aggregation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python ≥ 3.9 (tested through 3.14)
  • PyYAML ≥ 6, (runtime dependency)

docs.title: Dev Dependencies
docs.text: • mkdocs >=1.6, <2

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
pip install .

Development:

pip install -e ".[docs]" pytest
pytest                           # test suite
mkdocs serve                     # docs site at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict            # validate and build docs

docs.title: File formats
docs.text: YAML is the default and recommended format for configuration and character files. JSON is accepted as well, .json files and JSON strings load with the very same structure. There is no XML. The paper's AffectML documents are represented in YAML. See Configuration for the mapping.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text: The engine is deterministic and time-step driven: nothing happens between calls, and the same inputs at the same times always produce the same affective trajectories. There is no internal clock, no threads and no randomness, you decide how fast simulated time passes.

docs.title: Advancing time
docs.text:
There are three ways to move the simulation forward, all equivalent:

  • update(dt), advance every character by dt seconds; the natural call from a game loop, with your frame or tick delta.
  • step(n), advance in whole update periods (500 ms by default, the paper's rate).
  • run(seconds), simulate a stretch of time in period-sized slices; convenient in tests and offline simulation.

One update does three things per character, in order: age all active emotions and drop the fully decayed ones; recompute the virtual emotion centre from what remains; move the mood one step (pulled/pushed by the emotion centre, or drifting back to the default mood when no emotions are active). The engine also keeps a running total of simulated time.

Any step size works, the dynamics are calibrated in seconds, not in ticks, but very large steps make the mood's path coarser: a single ten-minute update moves the mood in one straight line, while the same ten minutes in half-second steps bends smoothly around a moving emotion centre. Frame-rate steps at 60 fps are perfectly fine and cheap.

docs.title: Fitting it into a game loop
docs.text:
Treat the affect engine like any other simulation system: give it time every tick, give it events when they happen, read it when you render or decide behaviour.

  • Time: call update with the frame delta each tick, or accumulate the delta and update in fixed 500 ms slices if you prefer a fixed affect rate alongside a variable frame rate.
  • Events: wherever your game already dispatches gameplay events (an insult, a victory, a threat appearing), add a call that lets the affected characters perceive it, either as a named event/act through their rules, or as a direct appraisal.
  • Output: when choosing an animation, a line of dialogue or an idle behaviour, read the character's mood word and dominant emotion at that moment.

To run affect faster or slower than real time, scale the dt you pass, because the model is calibrated in seconds, scaling time is exactly equivalent to scaling all three time constants together.

A worked game-loop pattern is on the Examples page.

docs.title: What a typical timeline looks like
docs.text:
With publication defaults, a single strong negative appraisal (a very undesirable event, desirability −0.8) plays out like this:

Time Emotions Mood 0 s Distress elicited at about 0.8 starts drifting towards the Distress point in PAD space 10 s decayed to about 0.4 (linear decay) still drifting, more slowly, the emotion centre's intensity fell with it 20 s fully decayed; the active set is empty begins the slow return to the default mood approx 20 min later back at the default mood

Two things follow from the calibration, and they are the heart of the model's feel:

  • A single emotion barely dents the mood. Twenty seconds of pull at intensity 0.8 moves the mood only about 0.03 PAD units. Moods are medium-term by construction, one insult does not ruin an afternoon.
  • A stream of similar emotions escalates the mood. Repeated appraisals keep the emotion centre alive; once the mood crosses the centre, the push phase drives it deeper into its octant. That is how repeated fear experiences take a character from slightly anxious through moderate to fully anxious, and why a character who has been mistreated for ten minutes stays hostile for a while even after the mistreatment stops.

docs.title: Multi-character scenes
docs.text: Every character appraises the same world input through its own rules, so a single perceived act fans out into different emotions per observer , the attacker, the victim and each bystander all react in character. Perception calls accept an optional list of characters, which is how you scope an input to, say, only the characters in the same room.

docs.title: Determinism, saving and restoring
docs.text:
• There is no randomness anywhere. The same calls in the same order with the same time steps reproduce identical states, replays and tests are exact.
  • A character's complete dynamic state is small: its mood point plus its active emotions (type, intensity values, age, cause). The affect-output snapshot is JSON-able and suits save games and telemetry; restoring exactly means recreating the characters and re-adding their active emotions with their ages.
  • Resetting a character drops its emotions and returns its mood to the default mood.

docs.title: Constraints and guarantees
docs.text:
• Update requires a non-negative time step; negative values are rejected.
  • The mood always stays inside the PAD cube (−1 to +1 on every axis).
  • Emotion intensities stay in [0, 1] and never fall below the character's personality baseline; an elicitation weaker than the baseline is raised to it and stays active for the decay time.
  • The engine is not thread-safe: drive one engine from one thread, or guard it with your own lock. Separate engines are fully independent.
  • A character's personality, baselines and default mood are fixed when the character is added; changing the shared configuration afterwards affects newly elicited emotions and the ongoing mood dynamics, but does not recompute those per-character constants.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Cost per update is proportional to characters × active emotions, with small constants, a handful of float operations per emotion and one square root per mood step. Emotion intensities are memoized per age and personality baselines are precomputed per character. Hundreds of characters at the 500 ms period is trivial; per-frame updates at 60 fps are fine too. Appraisal cost is proportional to the number of matching rules per perceived input.

docs.title: The Model
docs.text:
ALMA (A Layered Model of Affect, Gebhard, AAMAS 2005) simulates three interacting kinds of affect as they occur in human beings, distinguished by how long they last and what they influence:

Layer Duration Theory Bound to Role Emotions short-term (seconds) OCC (Ortony, Clore & Collins 1988) a specific event, action or object colour immediate reactions: facial expressions, gestures, wording Moods medium-term (minutes) Mehrabian's PAD temperament space nothing concrete, a longer-lasting stable affective state steer strategies: dialogue style, idle behaviour, posture Personality long-term (permanent) Big Five / Five Factor Model (McCrae & John 1992) the individual frames everything: the default mood and emotional dispositions

docs.title: How the layers interact
docs.text:
world input ──► appraisal rules ──► EECs ──► OCC rules ──► active emotions
                                                                │ decay
             personality ──► emotion baselines ─────────────────┤
                                                                ▼
             personality ──► default mood          virtual emotion centre
                                  │                             │
                                  ▼           pull / push       ▼
                            mood return  ◄──────────────────► mood
  1. World input (events, acts, displays) is appraised through each character's subjective rules into emotion eliciting conditions (EECs).
  2. The OCC rules turn EECs into active emotions with intensities, biased by personality baselines. Active emotions decay back to their baseline within the emotion decay time (default 20s).
  3. All currently active emotions form a virtual emotion centre in PAD space, which drags the mood around via the pull/push mood change function.
  4. Absent active emotions, the mood slowly returns to the personality-derived default mood.

docs.title: Layer 1: Emotions (OCC)
docs.text:
ALMA's "EmotionEngine" implements the OCC cognitive model of emotions. Here emotions are valenced reactions to events that concern the character, to actions of agents the character holds responsible, and to objects. Appraising these produces EEC variables. Their signs select among the 24 emotion types, and their absolute values determine intensity. See Appraisal for the full reference.

Each emotion type maps to a point in PAD space (paper, Table 2):

Emotion P A D Octant Admiration 0.5 0.3 -0.2 +P+A-D Dependent Anger -0.51 0.59 0.25 -P+A+D Hostile Disliking -0.4 0.2 0.1 -P+A+D Hostile Disappointment -0.3 0.1 -0.4 -P+A-D Anxious Distress -0.4 -0.2 -0.5 -P-A-D Bored Fear -0.64 0.60 -0.43 -P+A-D Anxious FearsConfirmed -0.5 -0.3 -0.7 -P-A-D Bored Gloating 0.3 -0.3 -0.1 +P-A-D Docile Gratification 0.6 0.5 0.4 +P+A+D Exuberant Gratitude 0.4 0.2 -0.3 +P+A-D Dependent HappyFor 0.4 0.2 0.2 +P+A+D Exuberant Hate -0.6 0.6 0.3 -P+A+D Hostile Hope 0.2 0.2 -0.1 +P+A-D Dependent Joy 0.4 0.2 0.1 +P+A+D Exuberant Liking 0.40 0.16 -0.24 +P+A-D Dependent Love 0.3 0.1 0.2 +P+A+D Exuberant Pity -0.4 -0.2 -0.5 -P-A-D Bored Pride 0.4 0.3 0.3 +P+A+D Exuberant Relief 0.2 -0.3 0.4 +P-A+D Relaxed Remorse -0.3 0.1 -0.6 -P+A-D Anxious Reproach -0.3 -0.1 0.4 -P-A+D Disdainful Resentment -0.2 -0.3 -0.2 -P-A-D Bored Satisfaction 0.3 -0.2 0.4 +P-A+D Relaxed Shame -0.3 0.1 -0.6 -P+A-D Anxious

docs.title: Decay
docs.text: An elicited emotion decays from its initial intensity back to its personality baseline within the emotion decay time (20s by default). The decay curve is linear by default and can also be exponential, hyperbolicus, or a sigmoid that starts slowly, speeds up in the middle and levels off at the end.

docs.title: Dominant emotion
docs.text: Emotions should not a priori influence behaviour measurably: only the most intense active emotion whose intensity exceeds a threshold (default 0.4) is reported as dominant_emotion for behaviour control. All active emotions, dominant or not, still drive the mood.

docs.title: Layer 2: Moods (PAD space)
docs.text:
Mood is a point in Mehrabian's three-dimensional pleasure–arousal–dominance space, each axis in [-1, 1]. The eight octants carry discrete mood names (paper, Table 1):

+P+A+D Exuberant -P-A-D Bored +P+A-D Dependent -P-A+D Disdainful +P-A+D Relaxed -P+A-D Anxious +P-A-D Docile -P+A+D Hostile

Mood strength is the Euclidean norm of the PAD vector. The longest distance inside an octant, √3, is divided into three equal parts: slightly [0, √3⁄3), moderate [√3⁄3, 2√3⁄3), fully [2√3⁄3, √3]. A mood of (0.25, −0.18, 0.12) reads slightly relaxed.

docs.title: The virtual emotion centre
docs.text: Every active emotion is a point in PAD space (via the table above). Their average position is the virtual emotion centre (VEC); its intensity is the average of the active emotions' intensities (max 1.0). The VEC jumps around erratically as emotions come and go, so it is not the mood itself, but the force that changes the mood smoothly.

docs.title: The pull and push mood change
docs.text:
• Pull phase, while the current mood lies between the PAD origin and the VEC, the mood is attracted towards the VEC.
  • Push phase, once the mood is beyond (or at) the VEC, it is pushed further into its current octant. A person's mood intensifies as they undergo experiences that reinforce it. Repeated similar emotions therefore escalate a mood from slightly to moderate to fully.

The intensity of the VEC determines the speed. At the maximum intensity setting, the mood travels the distance between the centers of two adjacent octants (1.0 PAD unit) within the mood transition time (which is 10 minutes by default)

docs.title: Mood return
docs.text: The mood tends to drift back to the default mood. The longest octant distance (√3) is travelled in the mood return time, 20 minutes by default. The return applies while no active emotions exist (can be changed by mood_return_mode="idle|always").

docs.title: Layer 3: Personality (Big Five)
docs.text: A character's personality is a Big Five profile, openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism, each trait in [-1, 1]. It influences the model in two ways.

docs.title: Default mood
docs.text:
Mehrabian's regression of the Big Five onto PAD defines the character's resting mood:

Pleasure  =  0.21·Extraversion + 0.59·Agreeableness + 0.19·Neuroticism
Arousal   =  0.15·Openness + 0.30·Agreeableness − 0.57·Neuroticism
Dominance =  0.25·Openness + 0.17·Conscientiousness
             + 0.60·Extraversion − 0.32·Agreeableness

The paper's worked example: openness 0.4, conscientiousness 0.8, extraversion 0.6, agreeableness 0.3, neuroticism 0.4 → default mood (P 0.38, A −0.08, D 0.50), octant Relaxed.

docs.title: Emotion baselines
docs.text: Personality biases emotion intensities with a baseline intensity per emotion type, "an extravert character's baseline intensity for joy is 0.15, whereas an introvert character's would be 0.0" (IVA'03). Elicited intensities are raised by the baseline, and emotions decay back to the baseline rather than to zero. The default weight table (positive emotions from extraversion + agreeableness, negative from neuroticism, small conscientiousness/openness terms for the attribution/attraction groups) is a documented interpolation from the papers' qualitative guidance, see Fidelity Notes.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: This page explains how you work with the engine, what the moving parts are and how they fit together. Examples for everything described here is collected on the Examples page.

docs.title: The engine and its characters
docs.text:
An AffectEngine owns any number of characters and the global computation parameters (an AffectConfig the defaults are the publication values).

Each character is added by name, together with two things that define who they are affectively:

  • a personality, a Big Five profile (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism), each trait between -1 and +1. The personality is fixed for the character's lifetime; the engine derives the character's default mood from personality, this is also the resting point the mood always drifts back.
  • an optional rule book, the character's subjective appraisal rules, which decides how the character interprets events, acts and their perception. Characters still work without rules, and appraisals can be feed directly.

A character starts in its default mood with no active emotions. You can also hand it a different starting mood if the scene calls for one.

docs.title: Two ways to feed the simulation
docs.text:
Direct appraisal: When the upstream logic already knows how something should feel, you tell a character directly: this was a moderately good event, that was a bad act by someone else. These judgements are expressed as emotion eliciting conditions, and constructors exist for all the standard cases (a good or bad event, a likely or unlikely future event and many others). The Appraisal page explains the vocabulary and exactly which emotion each judgement elicits.

Perceived world input: In multi-character scenes it is usually better to describe what happened once and let every character appraise it through its own rules. The engine accepts four kinds of world input:

  • a named event (e.g. "SunIsShining"), appraised by every character that has a basic rule for that name
  • an act with a performer and optional target ("Sven attacks Valerie"), the performer appraises it with its self rules, the target with its direct rules, and everyone else with their indirect (listener) rules;
  • an emotion display, a visible emotional cue such as shame, appraised by the displaying character (self) and by observers (other);
  • a mood display, a visible mood cue such as nervous idle behaviour, scoped the same way.

Because each character carries its own rules, one attack can leave the victim distressed and angry, the attacker gloating, and a bystander feeling pity, from a single call.

Both feeding styles return the emotions they elicited, so your downstream logic can react immediately to what a character just felt.

docs.title: Advancing time
docs.text: Nothing decays or drifts on its own, you advance simulated time explicitly. Call the engine's update() method with the seconds that passed or let it step in the paper's 500 ms periods. Each update ages and expires active emotions, recomputes the emotion centre and moves every character's mood. See Simulation for the dynamics and game-loop patterns.

docs.title: Reading the affect back
docs.text:
At any moment a character exposes its full affective state:

What Meaning Mood A point in PAD space, plus its readable description, octant word and strength, e.g. slightly hostile Default mood The personality-derived resting mood, for comparison Dominant emotion The most intense active emotion above the behaviour threshold, or none, the one emotion that should visibly drive behaviour Active emotions Every currently decaying emotion, with intensity and cause Emotion intensity The current level of any one emotion type (its personality baseline when not active) Affect output A JSON-able snapshot of all of the above, for saves, telemetry or debugging

The intended division of labour (from the paper's own system):

The dominant emotion drives short-lived, pointed behaviour, facial expressions, a spontaneous interjection, an emotional gesture. The mood drives everything slower, wording and phrasing, dialogue strategy, idle behaviour, posture, how forcefully gestures are performed. The mood word ("moderate exuberant") is designed to be switched on directly: eight octants and three strengths gives a standard vocabulary the further behaviours can branch over.

docs.title: Housekeeping
docs.text: Characters can be reset (emotions dropped, mood back to default), removed, or enumerated. Profiles, personality, rules, can be loaded from YAML (or JSON) files instead of being built in code. See Configuration.
